title: You expected blood on the gates. Steel against steel. A violent ending that made sense to human logic.
paragraphs: You expected blood on the gates. Steel against steel. A violent ending that made sense to human logic.
But that’s not how Jericho fell.
And that’s exactly the point.
Because what happened in Book of Joshua wasn’t just a military victory—it was a confrontation between human strength and divine authority. One of them had to be exposed.
You already know which one lost.
The city stood sealed. Massive walls. Generations of fear behind them. No breach points. No weak side. No chance—at least not by ordinary means.
And then God gave Joshua instructions that sounded almost offensive to logic.
Walk.
Just walk.
Circle the city once a day for six days. No shouting. No attack. No siege engines. Just obedience that looked like foolishness.
If you were there, you would have felt it. The tension. The silence. The watching eyes from the walls. The quiet humiliation of doing something that didn’t look like warfare at all.
Because God was stripping something away.
Not from Jericho.
From His own people.
“But here’s what most people don’t realize…”
God was never just trying to bring down walls.
He was tearing down their dependence on human strength.
If Israel had taken Jericho with swords, they would have believed the victory belonged to them. Their strategy. Their courage. Their skill.
And God refuses to share His glory with human pride.

Isaiah 42:8 says,
“I am the Lord; that is my name; my glory I give to no other…”
Read that again.
No other.
So instead of battle plans, God gave them a pattern that exposed the heart.
Because walking in silence forces you to confront what’s inside you.

Doubt starts talking.
Fear starts whispering.
Pride starts resisting.

“Why are we doing this?”
“This makes no sense.”
“This won’t work.”
God saw it.
You knew.
By the seventh day, something had shifted.
Not in the walls.
In them.
They weren’t relying on swords anymore. They were clinging to a word from God. And that’s when the command came:
Shout.
Not because shouting breaks stone.
But because faith had finally reached its breaking point.

Hebrews 11:30 says,
“By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.”
Not by force.
By faith.
The sound that brought Jericho down wasn’t just noise.
It was surrender.
It was trust reaching its peak. It was obedience refusing to turn back. It was a people finally realizing that victory doesn’t come from their hands—it comes from God alone.
And in that moment, the walls collapsed.
Not weakened.
Not cracked.
Collapsed.
Because when God moves, He doesn’t struggle.
Now look closer.
Because Jericho isn’t just history.
It’s a mirror.
There are walls in your life right now that you’ve been trying to fight with your own strength.

Habits you can’t break.
Sin you keep excusing.
Patterns you keep hiding.
You’ve been swinging swords at something God never told you to fight that way.
And it’s not working.
You know it.
“But here’s what most people don’t realize…”
God will sometimes remove your weapons… just to show you they were never the answer.

2 Corinthians 10:4 says,
“For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.”
Not of the flesh.

Not your effort.
Not your discipline.
Not your image.
Divine power.
And this is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because the same pride that wants to conquer Jericho with a sword… resists the idea of surrender.
You’d rather fight than submit.
You’d rather try harder than fall on your knees.
But your walls aren’t falling because you’re still trying to be the one who knocks them down.
This is where the Gospel steps in.
Because the greatest wall wasn’t Jericho.
It was the separation between you and God.

Isaiah 59:2 says,
“Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God…”
Sin built that wall.
And no amount of human effort could tear it down.
So God didn’t send a strategy.
He sent a Savior.
Jesus Christ didn’t circle your sin.
He crushed it.
At the cross, what you could never break—He destroyed.

Colossians 2:14 says,
“He canceled the record of debt… nailing it to the cross.”
That wall didn’t fall with noise.
It fell with blood.
And now you’re standing in the same place Israel stood.
A choice.

Keep trusting your own strength…
Or finally surrender to God’s way.
Because one leads to exhaustion.
The other leads to freedom.
Say it.
“I’ve been fighting the wrong way.”
Let that come out of you.
They need to see this.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—really deeper—into understanding Scripture, breaking strongholds, and walking in real discipleship, there’s a place for that.
Not for content.
For transformation.
Because walls don’t fall when you try harder.
They fall when you trust God completely.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
